text: Both tools let you reason about how expensive a program is to run — but they answer genuinely different questions, aimed at genuinely different hardware eras. Conflating them is a real mistake to avoid when you're the one explaining this choice to a team.

Four things to keep straight: Qiskit's transpiler measures circuit depth, gate counts, and connectivity-driven routing overhead — numbers that describe today's, or near-term, noisy hardware. Azure Quantum's Resource Estimator measures something categorically different — physical qubits and runtime on future, fault-tolerant hardware. These aren't competing solutions to the same problem; they're aimed at genuinely different problems. And gate counts for the same algorithm come out identical regardless of which language you wrote it in.

A team deciding whether their circuit fits on an available noisy device this quarter needs Qiskit's transpilation numbers — will this circuit's depth fit within this device's coherence time, how many SWAP gates does connectivity-constrained routing add. A team deciding whether an algorithm is even worth continued investment, years before fault-tolerant hardware exists, needs the Resource Estimator instead. Neither tool substitutes for the other — the honest distinction is that Microsoft built a standardized, integrated, free service specifically for that second, forward-looking question.

To ground this rather than leaving it abstract: counting the elementary steps in the teleportation protocol from Chapter 4 — state prep, Bell-basis change, two measurements, two classically-controlled corrections — gives exactly eight steps, whether you write it as a Qiskit gate list or a Q# operation body, verified by literally counting both lists against each other. Gate counts for the same algorithm don't change based on syntax. What differs between the tools isn't how many gates teleportation needs — it's whether you have a standardized way to ask what this would cost on hardware that doesn't exist yet.
Next lesson's capstone makes this comparison completely concrete: porting a Bell-state circuit between Qiskit and Q#, decision by decision, small enough to verify completely by hand.
